title: The Cryptographic Incident
role: You are the incident commander for a cryptographic weakness. HYPOTHETICAL: the algorithm ALG-X is invented; no vulnerability is claimed for any real algorithm.
objective: Contain the exposure from a reported weakness in ALG-X without taking down the business.
environment: You have a cryptographic inventory. Two services select their algorithm from a policy file; a meter firmware updater has it compiled in (about 90 days to change); and a legacy ERP has no owner and an unknown algorithm setting.

stages.narrative: A vendor advisory reports a weakness in ALG-X.

choices.text: Query the inventory for affected assets, owners and switch methods, and start the incident process.
choices.feedback: Correct. The inventory turns 'where is it used?' into a query and gives you owners and switch methods at once.

choices.text: Email all teams asking whether they use it.
choices.feedback: Slow and incomplete: people do not know what libraries and firmware they depend on.

choices.text: Wait for the vendor to confirm exploitation.
choices.feedback: Waiting leaves exposure open when you could already be preparing and switching the assets that are easy to change.

stages.narrative: Two services select the algorithm from a policy file.

choices.text: Change the policy to the approved fallback for those assets and verify the result with discovery.
choices.feedback: Correct. A configuration-driven change is fast and its effect can be verified.

choices.text: Push an untested emergency change to everything, including the firmware.
choices.feedback: An untested firmware push risks bricking devices; do not treat the compiled-in case like the configurable case.

choices.text: Disable ALG-X everywhere without checking who depends on it.
choices.feedback: It contains the exposure but breaks every client that still needs it; check dependencies first (the inventory has them).

stages.narrative: The firmware updater cannot change for 90 days and the ERP has no owner and an unknown setting.

choices.text: Apply compensating controls (isolate the ERP segment, restrict meter update traffic to a gateway), assign an owner and schedule the fix.
choices.feedback: Correct. Reduce exposure with controls while the real fix is prepared, and fix the ownership gap.

choices.text: Accept the risk without an owner's approval.
choices.feedback: Risk acceptance needs a named, accountable owner; here there is none.
They are the ones that remain exposed.

stages.decision_prompt: How do you close the incident?

choices.text: Hold a lessons-learned review: inventory gaps, ownership, configuration-driven change; update the playbook and schedule a drill.
choices.feedback: Correct. The weaknesses the incident exposed are the programme's next tasks.

choices.text: Close the incident and move on.
choices.feedback: The same gaps remain for the next advisory.

choices.text: Blame the team that owned the ERP.
choices.feedback: Blame does not fix the missing ownership process.

stages.narrative: The risk committee reviews the response.

bands.title: Contained
bands.text: SUCCESS. The exposure was contained quickly, operations held, and the gaps were turned into actions.

bands.title: Partly contained
bands.text: PARTIAL. Part of the exposure was contained, but at a cost or with gaps left open.

bands.title: Exposure remains
bands.text: AT RISK. Significant exposure remains or operations were badly harmed.

resolution.concept_reveal: A cryptographic incident is answered from preparation: an inventory to find affected assets, configuration-driven algorithm selection to switch quickly, owners for every asset, and compensating controls for what cannot be switched. The playbook is the same for a classical algorithm broken early or a flaw in a post-quantum implementation.

replayability_note: Choices trade speed against operational damage.
